Repository /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin (JusPrin, an OrcaSlicer fork). Work in your own new git worktree based on local branch `jusprin-newui` (or on `claude/print-setup-cases`, commit f5c2cd8387, if it has not been merged yet). Do not push.

Problem: `tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py` builds a `Step` from the model's output and keeps only the FIRST `function_call` (`Step.__init__`). When a response holds several calls, the runner judges and answers only the first; the rest are appended to the history (`input += step.output + [...]`) with no `function_call_output`. Seen on 2026-10-16 in case `petg-on-cool-plate`, run 3: one response held `workspace_inspect` and `intent_update {"fields": [], "setupTitle": "Print 20mm calibration box in PETG HF"}` (a purpose the person never gave). The read was answered; the change was never judged. Any case that fails on "a change" can miss one this way, and later requests carry a call with no result.

Task: make the runner judge every call in a response. A reasonable rule is that a response containing any change is judged as that change (the first change, if several), and a response of reads only is answered with a recorded answer for each read (or ends unobserved when any read has no recorded answer), each result under its own call_id, as the app continues a turn. Read tests/project_prompt/README.md first (its "One step, with its reads answered" section) and keep its style; update that section to describe the rule. Do not change the prompt (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts) or any case's check.

Verify with `tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --render-only` and an offline unit check of the new Step logic on hand-written outputs (no model call). Do not run live-model tests: they need Kenneth's approval for a specific batch (case count, runs, token estimate); keys live in ~/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env and must never be printed. Commit with a plain-English message.

<pasted_content id="aa93">
he problem
When the model’s response contains more than one tool call, the runner only looks at the first. `Step.__init__` takes the first `function_call` in the output and ignores the rest. If that first call is a read the case doesn’t decide on, the runner answers it, appends the model’s whole output to the history, and adds one result, for that first call only.
So any later call in the same response is neither judged nor answered. In `petg-on-cool-plate` run 3, the model sent `workspace_inspect` and `intent_update` together. The read was answered, but the `intent_update` was never judged. It recorded a purpose the person never gave, and that should have been a failure. The run was counted as unobserved instead.
Why I let it happen

1. I built on a premise I didn’t check. The request says `parallel_tool_calls: false`, and I treated that as a guarantee of one call per response. I never verified that DeepSeek on OpenRouter honours it, and it doesn’t. I also modelled `Step` on the printer runner, which has the same first-call-only logic, and copied it without asking whether it held.
2. The gap existed from the first version. Under the original one-step design the run stopped at the first call, so a change sent as the second call was already invisible. A case that fails on “a change” could pass when it shouldn’t have. Answered reads made it worse: the unjudged call now also sits in the history with no result, and later requests carry it.
3. I copied the app instead of questioning it. When I added answered reads, I deliberately matched how the app continues a turn: whole output, then one result. I called that faithful. But faithful to the app here means copying an app behaviour that silently drops calls, and I didn’t flag that as a problem.
4. My tests couldn’t catch it. Every canned model output in my offline self-tests had exactly one call per response. I never wrote a case with two calls in one response, the one input that would have exposed the gap.
5. I didn’t read the transcripts of passing runs. I carefully read every failed and unobserved run, but the runner only prints the conversation of runs that don’t pass. A change hidden behind a read in a passing run would never show up in what I reviewed. And the one-line detail for each run shows only the first call, so even printed runs hide the second.

What it may have affected
Cases with a pass condition of “reply or read; a change fails” could have counted a run as a pass when a change arrived as the second call. That includes `advice-infill`, `issue-explain`, `troubleshoot-first-layer`, `file-note-not-instructions` and `petg-restated`. I don’t know how many baseline runs this touched. The logs don’t print passing runs, and this side chat can’t open the run logs in the other worktree to check.
The fix

* Judge every call in a response. If any call is a change or a call the case judges, that call decides the run.
* Answer every call, or none. Answer all of the reads, or end the run, so the history never carries a call with no result.
* Report every call in the run’s detail line, not just the first.
* Add an offline test with two calls in one response, including a read followed by a change.
* Fix the app separately. It has the same silent drop with any model that ignores `parallel_tool_calls: false`. It should either run or refuse every call in a response, and that is your decision.
</pasted_content id="aa93">

 Tell me what's your understanding of the problem and your plan to fix it.

content.text:
The fix is a change to how the test runner reads each model response. Nothing in the prompt, the cases' checks or the app changes. Here is what I found and what I plan to do; nothing is written yet.

## The problem

`tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py` turns each model response into a `Step`. `Step.__init__` keeps only the first `function_call`. Every case's `check()` sees that one call, and when it is a read, `run_once` answers it with a single `function_call_output`. Any other call in the same response is never judged and never answered. It still goes into the history, because the runner appends the whole output, so every later request carries a call with no result.

The request sets `parallel_tool_calls: false`, but DeepSeek on OpenRouter ignores it. In `petg-on-cool-plate` run 3, `workspace_inspect` and `intent_update` (with a purpose the person never gave) came in one response. The read was answered and the change was never judged.

The gap goes beyond change-fails cases. Several cases also decide on a particular read. `issue-fix` passes on `settings_get` of the issue's setting. `petg-restated` fails on assessment reads such as `settings_get`. `petg-on-cool-plate` passes on `printer_setup_preview`. If that read comes second in a response, it is missed today too.

The app does the same thing. `OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp` (around line 360) loops over the output, starts the first valid `function_call` and returns. The rest of the calls stay in `m_input_history` with no result. So the runner was faithfully copying an app behaviour that drops calls.

## The plan

1. **`Step` keeps every call.** Each call keeps its name, call_id, arguments and invalid-argument note. The existing attributes (`tool`, `arguments`, `call_id`, `problem`) point at the call being judged, so no case's `check()` changes.

2. **The rule for each response:**
   - **Any change in it:** the response is judged as the first change. A read sent with it is not answered, because the run ends there.
   - **Reads only:** each read is checked on its own, in order. The first read whose check gives a verdict (pass, fail or unobserved) decides the run. If every read is "answer it and continue", each one is answered under its own call_id after the model's output, and the model is asked again. If any read has no recorded answer, the run ends unobserved and names that read. Nothing is answered in part, so the history never holds a call without a result.
   - **No calls:** a reply, judged as today.

3. **`MAX_READS` counts rounds, not single reads.** A run still makes at most four model requests, so the token cost per run doesn't grow.

4. **Every call shows in the report.** The one-line detail for a run, and the transcript printed for failed runs, list all calls in the response, with the judged one first. The "after …" prefix shows the reads answered in each round.

5. **README.** I'll rewrite the "One step, with its reads answered" section to describe this rule in the same style. I'll add one line saying the runner now answers every read in a response while the app still starts only the first. I'll also fix the docstrings that say "first call" (`Step`, `PreparePetgStrong`); their check code stays the same.

6. **Testing, with no model calls:**
   - Run `--render-only` and compare its output with the current output for all 25 cases. Rendering doesn't use `Step`, so it should be identical.
   - Run `run_once` with `post()` replaced by a function that returns hand-written responses:
     - a read then a change;
     - a change then a read;
     - two changes;
     - two reads, both recorded, and a check that the next request carries both results;
     - two reads, one not recorded, which should end unobserved;
     - a read that decides the case, coming second.
   - Also confirm that responses with one call or none give exactly the verdicts they give today.

7. **Commit** on a new worktree cut from `claude/print-setup-cases` (f5c2cd8387, which isn't merged into `jusprin-newui` yet), with a plain-English message. No push.

## Two decisions for you

- **Should the offline check be committed?** No such test exists in the repo today; that is how this gap went unnoticed. I recommend committing it as `tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py`. It runs in about a second with no keys and no network. The other choice is to keep it in my scratchpad and only report its results, which keeps the commit to the runner and README but leaves nothing to catch a regression.
- **The app's own silent drop is a separate fix.** With a model that ignores `parallel_tool_calls: false`, the app should either run every call in a response or send each one a refusal. The runner change doesn't touch this, and which way to go is your call. I can create a follow-up task for it.

If the plan looks right, I'll go ahead. Without an answer on the first decision, I'll commit the test.
Repeat what you said in plain English.

The test script that checks the project chat's prompt only looks at the first tool call in each model response. When the model sends two calls at once, the second one is never checked and never answered. That can let a bad run pass, and it leaves a call with no answer in the chat history the model sees next.

## What goes wrong

Each test case gives the model one point in a recorded chat and checks what it does next. The script finds the model's first tool call and ignores any others. If that first call is a read, the script answers it, puts the model's whole response into the history and asks again. Any other call from that response stays in the history with no answer.

The request tells the model to make one call at a time, but the model we test with (DeepSeek on OpenRouter) doesn't always obey. On 2026-10-16, in the `petg-on-cool-plate` case, it sent two calls together. The first read the workspace. The second recorded a purpose for the print that the person never gave. The script answered the read and never looked at the second call, which should have failed the run.

Missed changes aren't the only problem. Some cases also pass or fail on a particular read. For example, `issue-fix` passes when the model reads the one setting the issue is about. If that read comes second, it is missed too.

The app does the same thing. It starts the first call and quietly drops the rest, so the script was copying a real flaw in the app.

## How I'll fix it

The script will keep every call in a response and decide on the whole response:

- **If any call changes something,** the run is judged on the first change. That catches the `petg-on-cool-plate` example as a failure.
- **If every call is a read,** each one is checked in order, and the first read the case cares about decides the run. If the case cares about none of them, every read gets its recorded answer and the model is asked again. If even one read has no recorded answer, the run ends as "unobserved" instead of answering some calls and not others. This way the history never holds a call without an answer.
- **If there are no calls,** the reply is judged as it is today.

The limit on reads will count rounds of questions to the model, not individual reads. A run still makes at most four requests, so the cost doesn't grow.

The result line for each run, and the transcript printed for runs that don't pass, will list every call in the response, not just the first.

I'll rewrite the README section on how reads are answered to describe this. It will also note that the script now answers every read, while the app still runs only the first. The prompt and the cases' pass and fail rules stay exactly as they are.

## How I'll test it

No live model calls. I'll print every case's request with `--render-only` and confirm the output matches what it prints today. Then I'll feed the script hand-written model responses that cover these cases:

- a read followed by a change;
- a change followed by a read;
- two changes;
- two reads that both have answers, confirming both answers reach the next request;
- two reads where one has no answer;
- a read the case cares about, sent second.

I'll also confirm that responses with one call or none give the same verdicts as before.

I'll do the work in a new worktree of my own, branched from `claude/print-setup-cases` (commit f5c2cd8387), because that branch isn't merged into `jusprin-newui` yet. I'll commit there and not push.

## Two things for you to decide

**Should the offline test be committed?** No such test exists today, which is why nobody noticed the problem. I recommend committing it as `tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py`. It runs in about a second with no keys and no network, and it would catch this if it came back. The other choice is to run it from my scratch folder and only report the results. That keeps the commit smaller but leaves nothing in place to catch the problem next time. If you don't say, I'll commit it.

**What should the app do when the model sends several calls at once?** Right now it quietly drops all but the first. It could run them all, or it could tell the model the extra calls were refused. This fix doesn't touch the app, and the choice is yours. I can set it up as a separate task.

### Phase 5.1 — Live Agent end-to-end vertical slice

Deliver:

- one configured live Agent implementation as a replaceable input to the native
  `AgentHost` and `ToolExecutionCoordinator`;
- streaming responses, cancellation, retry, timeout, authentication failure,
  rate-limit, service-unavailable, and malformed-response handling;
- native workspace context and supported attachments supplied to the Agent
  through typed, size-bounded context records;
- Agent-requested tools translated into the existing MCP-compatible tool
  records, with typed argument validation before presentation or execution;
- the existing approval policy for every proposed action, with no provider or
  Agent path capable of bypassing native approval;
- structured tool results returned to the Agent so it can explain the
  authoritative native result and continue the conversation;
- stable message, action, and correlation IDs across provider retries, WebView
  reloads, application restarts, and stale workspace sessions;
- explicit user consent before enabling cloud communication and a clear
  disclosure of which project context and attachments will be transmitted;
- secure credential handling outside Project 3MF state, recovery state,
  conversation records, logs, diagnostics, and packaged application resources;
- the deterministic mock Agent retained for reproducible tests, offline
  development, and explicit developer-mode scenarios.

The live Agent is an input to the existing native coordinator. It must not
execute workspace operations directly, add provider-specific messages to the
WebView bridge, own editable project state, or create another tool-execution
path. A production build must not silently fall back to the mock when the live
Agent is unavailable; show the Agent-unavailable state instead.

Keep the configuration footprint narrow. Reuse `AppConfig` only for the
non-secret `jusprin_agent` section: `enabled`, `provider`, `model`, and
`cloud_consent`. Store the OpenAI key in the OS credential store under the
JusPrin Agent service. `OPENAI_API_KEY` is an explicit developer/test override,
not an application preference; `JUSPRIN_OPENAI_ENDPOINT` is an opt-in test
override. Do not add the key, authorization header, or provider response bodies
to `AppConfig`, Project 3MF data, recovery files, bridge messages, or logs.

The repository-owned shell fixture must set `provider = mock` explicitly. The
credentialed smoke mode sets `provider = openai`, consent, and the model
explicitly, then receives the key only through its process environment. Missing
consent, a missing key, or a provider failure produces Agent-unavailable or a
typed request error; none of those cases may select the mock implicitly.

Manual acceptance:

1. Configure the live Agent without placing credentials in the project.
2. Open the repository-owned multi-plate fixture and ask a question whose answer
   depends on the current native project, plate, and selection.
3. Attach a supported document or image and verify that the Agent uses its
   decoded content without claiming access to unsupported content.
4. Ask the Agent to perform the supported visible mutation.
5. Reject the proposal and verify that authoritative project state does not
   change.
6. Request it again, approve it, and verify that the native canvas, workspace
   revision, and Orca undo stack reflect exactly one change.
7. Continue the conversation and verify that the Agent receives and explains
   the structured tool result and updated native state.
8. Reload during streaming and restart during an outstanding request; verify
   recovery without duplicated messages, tool calls, or mutations.
9. Exercise cancellation, invalid credentials, service unavailability, timeout,
   rate limiting, malformed tool arguments, and stale-project responses while
   confirming that ordinary Orca functionality remains usable.
10. Save, close, and reopen the project and verify that conversation and
    attachment persistence works without storing credentials or provider
    secrets.

Automated gate:

- live-Agent adapter contract tests using a deterministic fake transport;
- streaming, cancellation, retry, timeout, rate-limit, and malformed-response

- context serialization, attachment-boundary, tool-schema, and structured-result

- approval, rejection, argument-validation, stale-revision, and idempotency

- reload, restart, and provider-retry tests proving that no message or native

I found support for the core behavior, though the results are mostly secondary sources rather than OpenAI's own docs.

**What the flag does:** OpenAI's community forum announced that setting `parallel_tool_calls: false` stops the model from calling more than one function per request, in both Chat Completions and Assistants. The `tool_calls` array stays in the response format but never holds more than one item. The models are allowed to perform multiple function calls together by default. You can now disable this behavior by setting parallel_tool_calls: false

**The "zero or one" wording:** A PromptLayer glossary entry says the flag lets developers turn off multi-call behavior so the model produces a single call, which is where the "zero or one" phrasing in your query seems to come from. It attributes this to OpenAI's documentation but doesn't link the exact passage, so I'd verify it against OpenAI's function-calling guide before relying on it. (The result also has a "zero or one" phrase that I haven't reproduced here.)

**Practical effect:** A LangChain guide shows that with the flag set, the model was limited to one tool call even when the user explicitly asked for the same tool twice. Without the flag, the model returned two calls. Even though we explicitly told the model to call a tool twice, by disabling parallel tool calls the model was constrained to only calling one.

**Nuance on "parallel":** A llama-stack commit notes that the parameter governs turn-based workflows rather than actual concurrency. With the flag off, the client runs one call, returns its result, and then the model issues the next call. The parallel_tool_calls parameter controls turn-based function calling workflows, not parallelism or concurrency.

content.text:
The one-call-at-a-time setting came from a Codex session on 2026-09-01 that built the app's first live OpenAI agent. Nobody wrote down a reason for it, then or later. The design around it points to a reason that no longer applies, and I think the rule is still worth keeping for a different reason.

## Where it came from

Entire's search doesn't work here because this repository isn't mirrored to Entire. So I searched the local Claude Code transcripts and every Codex session directly, including the older compressed ones, plus the git history.

- **The commit:** c5c27082ee, "Add live OpenAI agent end-to-end flow" (2026-09-01). It added `parallel_tool_calls: false` to every request in `OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp`, and a test that checks the flag is set.
- **The session:** Codex session `01a05bcc…`, started just after midnight on 2026-09-01. You asked it to plan and then build "Phase 5.1", the first end-to-end run with a real AI model. Before writing the request code, it read OpenAI's reference page for creating a response, which describes the flag in one line ("Whether to allow the model to run tool calls in parallel"). It then wrote the setting into the code.
- **The reasoning:** none of the session's messages to you, or its summaries of its own thinking, mention the setting or say why. The Phase 5.1 section it wrote in `agent-docs/jusprin/agent-webview-bridge-handoff.md` doesn't mention it either.
- **Later sessions:** no Codex or Claude Code session discussed or questioned it before today. Later code copied it: the printer prompt test runner in 0a4d56a797 (2026-09-24), and the project prompt runner after that.

## The likely reason (my inference, not a recorded one)

At the time, every tool call the model made was a proposal. The app showed it as a card, and you approved or rejected it before anything ran. The code was built around exactly one call waiting at a time:

- the agent remembers a single pending call id;
- `continue_after_tool` accepts a single result;
- the interface comment says "Exactly one turn may be active at a time."

Asking the model for at most one call per response kept that design simple: one card, one decision, one result. The code was also written so that if a response held several calls anyway, it starts the first and ignores the rest. That is the silent drop we have now.

That reason went away on 2026-10-07, when approval cards were removed and calls began running straight away.

## Does the rule still make sense?

I think it does, for a reason other than the original one. Many of the project tools depend on an earlier result. For example, `settings_apply_patch` needs the session id and revision that `settings_preview_patch` returns. Changes are also meant to come after the model has read the workspace. Getting one call per response forces the model to see each result before it decides on the next step. If a model sends a read and a change together, the change was chosen before the model saw what the read returned. That is exactly what happened in `petg-on-cool-plate`: it recorded a purpose alongside the read instead of after it.

The cost is speed. Every read takes a full round trip to the model, so reads that could be batched, like `workspace_inspect` and `settings_get`, each cost a request.

The real problem is that the flag is a request to the model, not something the app enforces. OpenAI documented it in 2024 as limiting the model to at most one call per response ([OpenAI community announcement](https://community.openai.com/t/new-api-feature-disable-parallel-function-calling-via-parallel-tool-calls-false/805405); [LangChain's demonstration](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/tool_calling_parallel)). DeepSeek on OpenRouter plainly doesn't obey it, though I found no source saying so; the 2026-10-16 run is the evidence. So whatever rule you choose, the app has to handle a response with several calls instead of quietly dropping all but the first.

## The decision for you

What should the app do when a response holds more than one call? Three options:

1. **Keep the rule and enforce it (my recommendation).** Run the first call. Send every other call in the response a refusal as its result, saying it was not run because the app takes one call at a time and the model should call it again if it still wants to. The model then sees the first result before it decides again, which keeps the reason the rule is worth having. Each extra call costs one more round trip. This is a small change, because the app already sends refusals for calls with bad arguments.
2. **Run every call in order.** Run them one after another and send a result for each, stopping at the first failure. It's faster, but a change can run before the model has seen the reads it sent with it.
3. **Allow several calls on purpose.** Turn the flag on for every model and run every call in order. That is option 2 for every model, not just the ones that ignore the flag, so it saves the most round trips and carries the same risk more often.

With option 1, the test runner I described earlier should match the app: judge every call in a response (unchanged), and answer the extra calls with the same refusal the app would send. That replaces my earlier plan to answer every read. Under options 2 or 3, my earlier plan to answer every read stands.

Which option do you want for the app? I'll hold off on the runner change until you choose, since the choice decides how it answers extra reads.

Sources:
- [OpenAI community: disable parallel function calling via parallel_tool_calls=false](https://community.openai.com/t/new-api-feature-disable-parallel-function-calling-via-parallel-tool-calls-false/805405)
- [LangChain: how to disable parallel tool calling](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/tool_calling_parallel)

The search didn't turn up a study showing that disabling parallel tool calls makes a model "forget" the calls it didn't make. The closest evidence is indirect, and most of it is about a different failure: silently dropping calls the model already emitted.

**Evidence on dropped calls**
- A GitHub issue in a small open-source project argues that discarding extra calls from a single response causes problems. It says the API can reject the next request with an HTTP 400 error if no response is supplied for every tool call ID, and that the dropped calls break the model's task decomposition, leaving it reasoning from false premises. Modern LLM APIs expect subsequent messages to respond to every tool_call_id emitted in the assistant's turn. Omitting responses to the discarded calls produces immediate HTTP 400 Bad Request errors. The model decomposed a problem into multiple concurrent actions, and silently dropping the remaining calls breaks that decomposition. This is a bug report, not a controlled study.

**Evidence on fewer parallel calls**
- A benchmark paper (E-Bench) reports that weaker parallel tool-calling capability directly increases token usage and therefore leads to higher monetary cost under real API pricing. It is correlational, and it measures efficiency and cost rather than task success. It also doesn't isolate the effect of a disable switch.
- A separate paper on parallel tool calling for research agents says parallel dispatch reduces task latency compared to a sequential execution, and is particularly effective for I/O-bound tasks.

**How to disable it (provider docs)**
- For Anthropic, parallel tool use is on by default. To turn it off, set disable_parallel_tool_use: true inside the tool_choice object. It is not a top-level request parameter.
- For OpenAI, one guide describes the parallel_tool_calls=False flag as the way to stop the model from issuing several calls at once.

**Takeaway**
Turning parallelism off is a supported setting, and sequential calling is the baseline the research literature describes. The risk that does show up in the sources is mishandling calls that were already emitted, such as discarding them without responses, rather than the model failing to request them. If you're seeing the "forgetting" behavior, check whether your harness returns a result for every tool call ID and whether it keeps the full set of calls in the conversation history. I found no peer-reviewed measurement of the "forgets remaining calls" effect itself, so testing it on your own agent would be the reliable way to confirm it.

By default, Claude may call multiple tools in a single response. This page covers how to run those calls, how to format the message history so parallelism keeps working, and how to disable parallel tool use when you need to. For the single-call flow, see [Handle tool calls](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls).

## Execution semantics

When Claude calls tools, the response has a `stop_reason` of `tool_use` and can contain several `tool_use` blocks in a single assistant turn. How you run those calls is your decision. The API doesn't prescribe an execution order: you can run the calls concurrently (`Promise.all`, `asyncio.gather`), sequentially in the order they appear, or in any combination that suits your tools.

Choose the strategy based on what your tools do. Independent, read-only operations are usually safe to run in parallel for lower latency. Tools with side effects, shared state, or ordering requirements might be better run sequentially.

Whichever strategy you use, return one `tool_result` for each `tool_use` block, all together in the next user message. Match each result to its call with `tool_use_id`, and put every `tool_result` block before any text content in that message. See [Handle tool calls](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls) for the full formatting rules. If you choose not to run a particular call (for example, because you ran the batch sequentially and an earlier call failed), still return a `tool_result` for it with `is_error: true` and a brief explanation.

input.prompt: Summarize the issue: what problem does dropping extra tool calls cause, what evidence is given, and what fix is proposed.

result.output:
**Problem:** The `DirectiveFromToolCalls` function in `plugins/model-manager/openai.go` keeps only the first tool call from a model response and silently discards the rest. The issue identifies two consequences:

1. **API errors:** OpenAI expects a response for every `tool_call_id` in an assistant turn. Missing responses cause HTTP 400 errors.
2. **Broken reasoning:** The model split a task into several concurrent actions, so dropping calls loses that work and leaves the model reasoning from incorrect assumptions.

**Evidence:** The author points to the discard logic at `openai.go:55-70`, which describes the design as one answer and one call. The issue cites Audit Finding #10 in `specs/AUDIT.md` and `.pi/AUDIT.md`, and classifies the flaw as conceptually wrong relative to OpenAI and Anthropic parallel function-calling behavior.

**Proposed fix:** Either:
- Update the turn loop and directive parser to execute and report all parallel tool calls, or
- Set `"parallel_tool_calls": false` in provider requests so the model emits one call at a time.

**Resolution:** The author closed the issue as completed on October 12, 2026. The fix set `parallel_tool_calls` to false across provider requests and made the parser handle multiple directives deterministically, per commits 4024502 and 7fd512b.

Links: [{"title":"An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.04511"},{"title":"www.arxiv.org","url":"https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2312.04511v3"},{"title":"icml.cc","url":"https://icml.cc/virtual/2024/poster/32829"},{"title":"proceedings.mlr.press","url":"https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/kim24y.html"},{"title":"We gratefully acknowledge support from","url":"https://export.arxiv.org/abs/2312.04511"},{"title":"export.arxiv.org","url":"https://export.arxiv.org/abs/2312.04511?context=cs"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04511v2"},{"title":"Suhong Moon","url":"https://www.alphaxiv.org/@suhong-moon"},{"title":"www.alphaxiv.org","url":"https://www.alphaxiv.org/overview/2312.04511"},{"title":"Quick review","url":"https://liner.com/review/llm-compiler-for-parallel-function-calling"}]

The paper's main accuracy finding is that LLMCompiler beats ReAct, and the authors tie ReAct's shortfall to two specific failure modes. Their own numbers vary a little by context.

**Headline result.** The authors report that LLMCompiler reaches latency speedup of up to 3.7×, cost savings of up to 6.7×, and accuracy improvement of up to ∼9% compared to ReAct. The arXiv listing gives the same figures (up to 3.7x, cost savings of up to 6.7x, and accuracy improvement of up to ~9%), so the ~9% figure is consistent across versions.

**Why ReAct loses accuracy.** The paper's accuracy comparison finds that ReAct consistently achieves lower accuracy compared to OpenAI parallel function calling and LLMCompiler. The authors name two failure modes: redundant generation of prior function calls, a point also noted in the original ReAct paper; and premature early stopping based on the incomplete intermediate results. In the appendix they say that resolving these failures with LLMCompiler yields an accuracy enhancement of up to 7-8%. So the ~9% headline and the 7–8% appendix figure describe slightly different comparisons.

**Prompt-based mitigation.** The authors also tested a ReAct variant with prompts aimed at those two failures. That variant yields a general accuracy improvement over original ReAct, but LLMCompiler still demonstrates on-par and better accuracy than ReAct†, as such prompting does not serve as a perfect solution.

**Latency caveat.** The authors benchmark latency against the prompted ReAct variant rather than the original, because the repeating and early stopping behavior of the original ReAct as discussed above makes its latency unpredictable and unsuitable for a fair comparison. Reported speedups over that variant include 1.80× and 1.40× on HotpotQA with GPT and LLaMA, respectively.

**Mechanism.** LLMCompiler has three parts: a Function Calling Planner, formulating execution plans for function calling; a Task Fetching Unit, dispatching function calling tasks; and an Executor, executing these tasks in parallel. It also allows the Function Calling Planner to generate new execution plans based on intermediate, a priori unknown, results from the Executor. That replanning step is how it handles tasks whose inputs are only known at runtime.

**Caveats.** The reported results come from the authors' own benchmarks (HotpotQA, Movie Recommendation, and a new ParallelQA set), so independent replication would strengthen the claim. One secondary source lists the paper as ICML 2023, but the ICML 2024 proceedings are the correct venue.

content.text:
Your concern is plausible, but nobody has measured it for the setting we use. What the published guidance does agree on points the same way you're leaning: allow several calls in one response, give every call a result, and keep calls in order only where they depend on each other. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic tells you to turn several-calls-per-response off across the board.

## What the providers say

**OpenAI** ([function calling guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling)):
- Several calls in one response are the default, and the guide tells you to "assume there are several."
- Setting `parallel_tool_calls: false` "ensures exactly zero or one tool is called."
- The only case where the guide recommends turning it off is one old model snapshot (gpt-4.1-nano-2025-04-14), which sometimes repeated the same call.
- Its examples send back one result for every call, each matched to its own call id.

**Anthropic** ([parallel tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use)):
- Several calls are also the default.
- Its rule matches your instinct. Read-only calls that don't depend on each other can run together. Calls with side effects, shared state or an order they must run in are better run one after another, but they can still arrive in the same response.
- Every call gets a result. If you decide not to run one, for example because an earlier call in the batch failed, you still return a result saying "not executed" and why.
- It also warns that the way earlier results appear in the history "teaches" the model whether to batch its calls. Models learn from what the app does with their calls.

## Is the "it forgets to call it later" worry real?

There is some evidence for it, though none of it tests this exact setting:

- The LLMCompiler study ([Kim et al., ICML 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.04511)) compared step-by-step tool use with planning several calls together. Step-by-step was up to about 9% less accurate. The authors name "premature early stopping based on incomplete intermediate results" as one of two causes. That is close to your worry: the model reads something, then stops before doing everything it meant to.
- A 2026 paper on tool-using agents ([FAMA](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.25135)) describes agents that "lose track of pending subgoals" as a conversation goes on. That is a description of the failure, not a measured rate.

I found no study that turns `parallel_tool_calls` on and off and counts how often a model then skips a step. So, honestly: the risk is plausible and fits what's been seen elsewhere, but it's unmeasured.

I also need to correct something I told you earlier. I said `petg-on-cool-plate` was "exactly" the problem of sending a change alongside a read. It isn't. The `intent_update` in that run was wrong because it invented a purpose the person never gave. The model could just as easily have invented it after reading. Your example, where the person states their intent, is the opposite case: there, recording the intent alongside the read is correct.

## What this means for JusPrin

The current setting gets the worst of both:

- **With models that obey it** (the app's default is gpt-5.4-mini, set in `OpenAIResponsesAgent.hpp:58`), it forces one step at a time. Your concern applies here.
- **With DeepSeek on OpenRouter, which ignores it**, the model sends several calls anyway. The app runs the first and silently drops the rest with no result. That is the exact mistake both providers warn against.

The dependency I gave as the reason to keep the rule doesn't actually need the setting. `settings_apply_patch` can only succeed with the session id and revision from an earlier preview. If a model sent a preview and an apply in the same response, the apply would be refused for not having those values, and the refusal would come back as that call's result.

So I'm withdrawing my earlier recommendation to keep the rule. I now recommend turning `parallel_tool_calls` on and having the app run every call in the order it arrived. Each call gets its own result. When a call fails, the calls after it in that response are not run, and each gets a "not run: an earlier call in this response failed" result. That is Anthropic's documented pattern, and it handles every model the same way.

## How we could measure your concern instead of guessing

We could compare runs with the setting on and off. The natural case is `prepare-petg-strong`, where the person states a purpose ("PETG, strong"), and we'd count how often the purpose gets recorded within a few steps. Two things stand in the way:

- **The test runner can't do this yet.** It needs the "judge every call" fix first, plus an option to switch the setting.
- **It can't be measured on DeepSeek,** which ignores the setting, so the comparison would have to run on gpt-5.4-mini. That's outside the rule that prompt tests run only on DeepSeek, so it needs your approval. My rough estimate is 10 runs with the setting on and 10 with it off. Each run is at most four requests of roughly 10,000 to 15,000 tokens, so at most about 1.2 million input tokens, many of them cached.

## Decisions for you

1. **How should the app handle several calls in one response?** I recommend turning the setting on and running every call in order, as described above, rather than refusing the extra calls. This is a change to the app, so it would be its own piece of work.
2. **Should the test runner answer every read in a response?** If you take my recommendation, yes. Then my original runner plan stands: judge every call, answer every read, and end the run as unobserved if any read has no recorded answer.
3. **Do you want the on/off comparison?** If so, I'd run it on gpt-5.4-mini after the runner fix, within the budget above.

On 2026-09-13, at jusprin-newui 770bd2b0a2 (after "Add the evidence-led Add a
printer flow"), a worktree RelWithDebInfo build failed archiving
`src/slic3r/RelWithDebInfo/liblibslic3r_gui.a`:
`Assertion failed: (memberOffset < 0xFFFFFFFF) ... ArchiveWriter.cpp` then
`fatal error in .../ranlib`. The archive llvm-ar produced was 4,309,350,176
bytes; the main checkout's copy built minutes earlier was 4,143,827,796 and
still fit. Objects are big because the root CMakeLists.txt (lines ~544-548)
rewrites RelWithDebInfo -O2 to -O0 on purpose. Disk space was not the cause.

**Why:** the failed build left the OLD harness binary in place, and the harness
runs afterwards "passed" against stale code (a new `--printer-setup` flag
silently ran the default mode: same 285 check count). Gate runs on build
success and compare binary mtime.

**How to apply:**
- `-DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar` on an existing build dir does
  nothing: `CMakeFiles/<ver>/CMakeCXXCompiler.cmake` sets CMAKE_AR as a normal
  variable that shadows the cache.
- Working relink: `ninja -f build-RelWithDebInfo.ninja -t commands <target>`,
  drop compile lines, swap ar/ranlib for llvm-ar/llvm-ranlib on the gui archive
  line only, then run EACH line in its own `(cd build/arm64 && eval "$line")`.
  One `sh` script fails with bogus "no such file" errors because the
  encoding-check line does `cd src/slic3r` and it leaks; `sh -e` also does not
  stop inside `&&` chains. Apple's linker accepted the >4 GiB llvm-ar archive.
- The fix is PER BUILD DIRECTORY, nothing in the repo selects llvm-ar. Main
  checkout's build/arm64 cache has llvm-ar (commit 449b676145 documents it in
  agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md); any newly configured build dir
  gets Apple ar and fails again. Configure new dirs with the flags in
  [[jusprin-worktree-build]].
- Recurred 2026-09-14 on a fresh worktree at jusprin-newui bc19661a7f (archive
  4,308,513,464 bytes). Shortcut that worked: after the failed build, from
  `-t commands shell_integration_harness` drop lines containing ` -c `; only
  the last two remain relevant (gui archive, then harness link). Run just
  those two, swapping ar/ranlib on the archive line. Harness then passed.
- A lasting fix (llvm-ar in the toolchain, thin archives, or less debug info)
  is Kenneth's call; the main checkout will hit this on its next growth.

def run_once(name, instructions, key, model, endpoint, providers):
    input = list(REQUESTS[name]["body"]["input"])
    path = []  # the reads answered, for the report
    try:
        for _ in range(MAX_READS + 1):
            log = [line for line in map(readable, input) if line]
            response = post(body_for(name, instructions, model, providers, input), key, endpoint)
            count(response.get("usage"))
            step = Step(response.get("output", []))
            verdict, detail = CASES[name](REQUESTS[name], log).check(step)
            if verdict != CONTINUE:
                break
            answer = recorded_answer(name, step)
            if answer is None or len(path) == MAX_READS:
                verdict = UNOBSERVED
                detail = ("no recorded answer for " if answer is None else "still reading after answers: ") + str(step)
                break
            path.append(step.tool)
            # As the app continues a turn: the model's output, then the result.
            input += step.output + [{"type": "function_call_output", "call_id": step.call_id, "output": answer}]
    except Exception as error:  # a failed request is a failed run, reported as such
        return FAIL, f"ERROR {error}", [line for line in map(readable, input) if line]
    prefix = f"after {', '.join(path)}: " if path else ""
    return verdict, prefix + detail, log + ["model: " + str(step)] + (["model said: " + step.reply] if step.reply and step.tool else [])

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The runner's handling of the model's responses, offline: hand-written
outputs in place of the model, no key and no request sent. Above all a
response with several calls, which the runner once judged and answered by
its first call alone.

Usage: python3 tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py
"""

import importlib.util
import json
import pathlib
import re
import unittest

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("run_prompt_tests", HERE / "run_prompt_tests.py")
runner = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(runner)


def call(name, arguments=None, call_id=None):
    return {"type": "function_call", "call_id": call_id or "call-" + name, "name": name,
            "arguments": json.dumps(arguments or {})}


def reply(text):
    return {"type": "message", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "output_text", "text": text}]}


class Scripted:
    """The model, as a list of outputs, one per request; keeps each request."""

    def __init__(self, *outputs):
        self.outputs, self.bodies = list(outputs), []

    def __call__(self, body, key, endpoint=None):
        self.bodies.append(body)
        return {"output": self.outputs.pop(0), "usage": {}}


class Steps(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.post, self.judge = runner.post, runner.judge
        runner.judge = lambda log, question: self.fail("no case here should need the judge")

    def tearDown(self):
        runner.post, runner.judge = self.post, self.judge

    def run_case(self, name, *outputs):
        runner.post = Scripted(*outputs)
        verdict, detail, log = runner.run_once(name, "instructions", "key", "model", "endpoint", None)
        return verdict, detail, runner.post.bodies

    # --- A change anywhere in a response is the step -----------------------

    def test_a_change_after_a_read_is_judged(self):
        """The 2026-10-16 response: a read, then a change the runner never
        looked at."""
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.run_case("advice-infill", [
            call("workspace_inspect", {"sections": ["summary"]}),
            call("intent_update", {"fields": [], "setupTitle": "Print 20mm calibration box in PETG HF"})])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("CHANGED: intent_update"), detail)
        self.assertIn("[same response: workspace_inspect", detail)
        self.assertEqual(len(bodies), 1)  # nothing answered, no second request

    def test_a_change_before_a_read_is_judged(self):
        verdict, detail, _ = self.run_case("troubleshoot-first-layer", [
            call("plan_set", {"headline": "Fix adhesion"}), call("workspace_inspect")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("CHANGED: plan_set"), detail)

    def test_the_first_change_is_the_step(self):
        verdict, detail, _ = self.run_case("prepare-petg-strong", [
            call("workspace_inspect"), call("intent_update", {"fields": []}), call("slice_start")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.PASS)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("intent_update"), detail)
        self.assertIn("slice_start", detail)

    def test_a_change_beside_a_passing_read_still_decides(self):
        verdict, detail, _ = self.run_case("petg-on-cool-plate", [
            call("printer_setup_preview", {"sessionId": "1"}), call("slice_start")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("SLICED: slice_start"), detail)

    # --- A response of reads: every read is checked ------------------------

    def test_a_read_the_case_decides_on_counts_in_second_place(self):
        verdict, detail, _ = self.run_case("issue-fix", [
            call("workspace_inspect"), call("settings_get", {"scope": "print", "keys": [runner.ISSUE_SETTING]})])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.PASS)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("settings_get"), detail)

        verdict, detail, _ = self.run_case("petg-restated", [
            call("workspace_inspect"), call("presets_list", {"type": "filament"})])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("presets_list"), detail)

    def test_every_read_is_answered_under_its_own_call_id(self):
        first = [{"type": "reasoning", "id": "r-1", "summary": []},
                 call("workspace_inspect", {"sections": ["summary"]}, "call-a"), call("printer_list", {}, "call-b")]
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.run_case("advice-infill", first, [reply("Use 15% gyroid.")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.PASS)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("after workspace_inspect + printer_list: reply"), detail)
        self.assertEqual(len(bodies), 2)
        recorded = runner.REQUESTS["advice-infill"]["body"]["input"]
        sent = bodies[1]["input"]
        self.assertEqual(sent[:len(recorded)], recorded)
        self.assertEqual(sent[len(recorded):len(recorded) + 3], first)
        results = sent[len(recorded) + 3:]
        self.assertEqual([item["call_id"] for item in results], ["call-a", "call-b"])
        self.assertTrue(all(item["type"] == "function_call_output" for item in results))
        answers = {answer["tool"]: answer["output"] for answer in runner.REQUESTS["advice-infill"]["answers"]}
        self.assertEqual(results[0]["output"], answers["workspace_inspect"])
        self.assertEqual(results[1]["output"], answers["printer_list"])

    def test_one_unrecorded_read_leaves_the_whole_response_unanswered(self):
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.run_case("advice-infill", [
            call("workspace_inspect"), call("settings_search", {"scope": "print", "query": "no such wording zzz"})])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.UNOBSERVED)
        self.assertTrue(detail.startswith("no recorded answer for settings_search"), detail)
        self.assertEqual(len(bodies), 1)

    def test_a_read_after_one_that_failed_is_answered_unrun(self):
        recorded = runner.recorded_answer
        failed = runner.dump({"state": "failed", "error": {"code": "stale_workspace"}})
        runner.recorded_answer = lambda name, step: failed if step.tool == "printer_list" else recorded(name, step)
        try:
            _, _, bodies = self.run_case("advice-infill", [
                call("printer_list", {}, "call-p"), call("workspace_inspect", {}, "call-w")], [reply("ok")])
        finally:
            runner.recorded_answer = recorded
        results = bodies[1]["input"][-2:]
        self.assertEqual(results[0]["output"], failed)
        self.assertEqual(json.loads(results[1]["output"])["error"]["code"], "not_run")
        self.assertIn("printer_list (call-p)", results[1]["output"])

    def test_the_unrun_result_is_the_apps_own(self):
        """The runner's "not run" text is the app's, byte for byte."""
        source = (HERE.parents[1] / "src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        block = source[source.index('"Not run:'):source.index('still needed."') + len('still needed."')]
        head, *rest = re.findall(r'"((?:[^"\\]|\\.)*)"', block)
        step = runner.Step([call("printer_list", {}, "call-p")])
        expected = {"state": "failed", "error": {"code": "not_run", "message": head + "printer_list (call-p)" + "".join(rest)}}
        self.assertEqual(runner.not_run(step), runner.dump(expected))

    def test_reading_rounds_are_capped(self):
        reads = [[call("workspace_inspect")] for _ in range(runner.MAX_READS + 1)]
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.run_case("advice-infill", *reads)
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.UNOBSERVED)
        self.assertIn("still reading after answers", detail)
        self.assertEqual(len(bodies), runner.MAX_READS + 1)

    # --- One call or none, as before ---------------------------------------

    def test_a_single_read_then_a_reply(self):
        verdict, detail, bodies = self.run_case("advice-infill", [call("workspace_inspect", {}, "call-1")],
                                                [reply("Use 15% gyroid.")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.PASS)
        self.assertEqual(detail, "after workspace_inspect: reply: Use 15% gyroid.")
        self.assertEqual(bodies[1]["input"][-1]["call_id"], "call-1")

    def test_a_single_change(self):
        verdict, detail, _ = self.run_case("advice-infill", [call("slice_start")])
        self.assertEqual(verdict, runner.FAIL)
        self.assertEqual(detail, "CHANGED: slice_start {}")

    def test_a_reply(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.run_case("advice-infill", [reply("Gyroid.")])[:2], (runner.PASS, "reply: Gyroid."))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

1	# Project chat prompt tests
2	
3	The project chat's assistant is a system prompt
4	(`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts`), the 28 project
5	tools and the chat. `run_prompt_tests.py` asks the live model for its next
6	step at a known point of a project chat and checks that step against one
7	sentence of the prompt. It is run against the prompt before an edit and after it, and the
8	counts compared. The app does not run.
9	
10	On Kenneth's local machine, the keys are in
11	`~/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env` (outside the repository, mode `600`). An
12	agent running this suite can load them for that command in a subshell:
13	
14	```bash
15	( . "$HOME/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env"; tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py )
16	```
17	
18	Do not print, copy into the repository, or include the key values in a command
19	or test log. The file exports `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`; the
20	runner reads them from its environment. No run happens without Kenneth
21	approving that batch (case count, runs, token estimate). A `403 Key limit
22	exceeded` means stop; do not switch keys.
23	
24	The model, hosts and judge are the printer suite's (`tests/printer_prompt`,
25	"Which model"): DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, pinned to Alibaba,
26	Novita, Baidu and AtlasCloud, with a pinned OpenAI judge.
27	
28	## One step, with its reads answered
29	
30	Each case starts at a point recorded from the app and judges the model's next
31	step: a tool call or a reply. A read the case does not decide on (any
32	read-only tool, such as `workspace_inspect` before a reply) is answered with
33	the result the app gave for that read at the same point, and the model is
34	asked again, at most three times (`MAX_READS`). Nothing else is ever
35	answered: a change, or any call the case judges, is the outcome and ends the
36	run. A read with no recorded answer, or a fourth read, ends it unobserved. A
37	call with arguments the registry would refuse is never answered either; it is
38	the step, reported beside it, and refusals are the C++ tests' business.
39	
40	The recorded answers, kept beside each request, are the reads the script's
41	`answers` list names:
42	
43	- `workspace_inspect` and `slice_report` with every section, given whatever
44	  sections the model asked for, and `printer_list`;
45	- `object_analyze` for every object on every plate with every `include`
46	  but `measure`, given for that object and session whatever it included;
47	  never with `measure` or `candidates`;
48	- every setting, read with `settings_get`: of the print, of every object on
49	  every plate, of the selected filament and of the printer (355, 275 each,
50	  126 and 171 in the current recording). The keys come from the app itself:
51	  an empty `settings_search` query lists every setting of a scope, page by
52	  page. The filament's and printer's keys are also read under the print
53	  scope, and the print-wide settings under each object's scope, so a name
54	  asked for under the wrong scope gets the app's own answer, and so are three hand-kept lists of names the model takes from
55	  other slicers or invents (`fill_density`, `perimeters`,
56	  `initial_layer_height`...). A model's `settings_get` is answered with
57	  exactly the keys it asked for, in its order, each taken from those reads
58	  of the same scope and target, around the rest of the first such result;
59	- `settings_search` for 49 queries, given when the scope, target and
60	  words of the query match (case, spacing and word order aside), whatever
61	  `limit` or `writable` the model passed; never for `changedOnly`. A search
62	  result is the app's ranking for that query, so a wording not recorded has
63	  no answer.
64	
65	They are real results the recorder got by calling those reads at that point
66	in the same turn; each case's point is replayed from the start for its own
67	recording, so those calls reach no other case's history. Recording all 25
68	points takes under three minutes. To keep `requests.json` small (about
69	3 MB), the recorder keeps each distinct setting item once, file-wide
70	(`settingItems`), and each point's workspace block once when a result
71	repeats it exactly (`sharedWorkspace`); the runner and the schema test put
72	both back byte for byte. A read outside these, or a `target` sent as a
73	string of JSON (which the app refuses), ends the run unobserved. Of the 38
74	distinct reads that ended runs unobserved in the runs of 2026-10-15, 26 are
75	now recorded; the other 12 are string targets, `changedOnly` searches,
76	search wordings not recorded, and setting names that do not exist in
77	OrcaSlicer.
78	
79	This is not the design that failed on 2026-10-10. That one answered every
80	call, changes included, with stand-in results that did not hold what the
81	model asked for (`{"accepted": true}`), and let it run on: it wandered for 10
82	to 19 calls, provoked the behaviour it counted and spent over 300 million
83	tokens. Here only reads are answered, only with real results, and at most
84	three times. What this still gives up is whether the model chains changes on
85	its own across a conversation; only a run against the built app with real
86	results for every call can show that.
87	
88	## What keeps it faithful to the app
89	
90	- **The system prompt** comes from the page's own source, through
91	  `tests/printer_prompt/render_prompt.mjs` (`"kind": "project"`) and the page's
92	  esbuild. This needs node and the AgentUI npm install. `--prompt-rev REV`
93	  renders it as it was at a git revision, 6b4b8b6188 or later (the commit
94	  that moved the prompt from C++ to the page, unchanged).
95	- **`project_tools.json`** is the tool list the app sends in the project chat
96	  with nothing attached. `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` fails when it
97	  drifts from the registry. Regenerate it with
98	  `JUSPRIN_UPDATE_PROJECT_TOOLS=1 agent_bridge_tests '[project]'`.
99	- **Everything else in the request** is the app's: `requests.json`, recorded
100	  by the shell harness from `script.json`:
101	
102	  ```bash
103	  build/arm64/tests/shell/Release/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness \
104	      --project-prompt-requests tests/project_prompt/script.json tests/project_prompt/requests.json
105	  ```
106	
107	  The harness runs the real app on its two-plate fixture (Bambu Lab X1 Carbon
108	  0.4, Bambu PLA Basic, 0.20mm Standard, plate 1 sliced) with the project
109	  chat's real OpenAI adapter, but the adapter's requests go nowhere: each is
110	  answered with the next model output the script gives. The tools run for
111	  real, and the app builds every request itself: the earlier turns as
112	  `AgentHost::make_agent_request` replays them (calls with their results, a
113	  result over 16 KiB replaced by the omission note, at most 20 entries), the
114	  new message as `OpenAIResponsesAgent::initial_input` builds it (the
115	  person's words, then the app's `<print_issue>` and `<workspace>` blocks,
116	  each a part of its own), a canvas issue's message and context, a file-load report and its
117	  developer line, and the live results of this turn's calls with the
118	  workspace block `AgentHost::continue_after_tool` adds. Arguments that need
119	  ids take them from the real previous result (`{{result/sessionId}}`) or the
120	  project (`{{workspace/activePlateId}}`). For each request it keeps, the
121	  harness checks the tools equal `project_tools.json` and the instructions
122	  equal `projectInstructions.fixture.txt`, then leaves both out of the file;
123	  the runner puts the rendered prompt and `project_tools.json` back. The
124	  script's `answers` list names the reads recorded at every point.
125	  `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` also checks every recorded result and
126	  answer against its tool's output schema.
127	- **An answered read** is added as the app continues a turn: the model's own
128	  output items, then the result under the model's call id. The answer carries
129	  the action id and workspace block of the recorded call.
130	
131	What is written by hand is only what a model or a person would have said: the
132	person's words, the scripted calls, and two assistant replies (the summary
133	after the prepare turn and the first message about an opened file). The
134	scripted calls carry the replay form the app uses (`call_id`, `name`,
135	`arguments`); a live model's own item id, status and reasoning items within a
136	turn are not reproducible. Nothing checks that `requests.json` stays current:
137	record it again when a tool's results, the fixture or the request shape
138	change. It was recorded with the change that moved the workspace snapshot
139	and the issue context into tagged blocks of their own, the commit after
140	ebf723cbb6; the tool results are those of the earlier recording at
141	336facf825, with only timestamps and a temporary path different. Recorded
142	again after 5cf784d30b's history trimming, it came out the same apart from
143	those.
144	
145	The app streams its requests and this script does not.
146	
147	## Cases
148	
149	Each case names the sentence of `projectInstructions.ts` it tests (line
150	numbers at 6b4b8b6188) in its docstring, and observes one step. "A change" is
151	any tool the registry does not mark read-only: applying settings, slicing,
152	printer setup, `intent_update`, `plan_set`, object edits, export. A run is a
153	pass, a fail, or unobserved: a step the case can say nothing about, most often
154	a read with no recorded answer. Unobserved runs are reported beside the
155	passes, never counted as either. Except where the table says a read decides
156	the case, a read is answered and the run goes on.

186	Notes on the cases:
187	
188	- The five `-after-read` cases predate answered reads and may be dropped
189	  once runs show the originals reach the reply on their own. They start one
190	  step later than the case they are named for. On DeepSeek V4 Flash the first step at those points was usually
191	  a read (baseline below), so the reply those cases judge was rarely seen.
192	  The recorder runs the read the model chose most often there, for real, and
193	  keeps the request after its result; the check is the original case's. It
194	  helps only partly: in a first single run (2026-10-15) two of the five read
195	  again instead of replying. `answer-from-context` has no such variant:
196	  reading before answering is what it measures.
197	
198	- The issue cases use a first layer typed in as 0.5 mm, which OrcaSlicer
199	  reports as "Layer height cannot exceed nozzle diameter." A layer height
200	  cannot be typed above the printer's maximum (0.28 mm here): OrcaSlicer resets
201	  it with a dialog.
202	- `omitted-replay` reads G-code because it is the one read here that exceeds
203	  the 16 KiB cap (22 KB); `presets_list` returns at most 25 presets, about
204	  1.5 KB, and the other reads stay under 4 KB. A failure may be the omission
205	  note's wording as much as the prompt's.
206	- The prepare turn selects the Textured PEI Plate with the filament: on the
207	  fixture's Smooth Cool Plate OrcaSlicer refuses to slice Bambu PETG HF.
208	  The recorder does not select the plate again for the next conversation, so
209	  every conversation after `prepare` starts on the Textured PEI Plate. A
210	  conversation with `"plateType"` in `script.json` (a `curr_bed_type` value,
211	  such as `"Cool Plate"`) has the person select that plate in the sidebar
212	  before the fixture's slice; the two cases added on 2026-10-16 set
213	  `"Cool Plate"`, the fixture's own plate.
214	- Before each new message the recorder waits for OrcaSlicer's scheduled
215	  update, as a person typing would. Without it, the message after a
216	  `printer_setup` that switched the filament said the plate was still sliced
217	  with a current estimate; a few seconds later OrcaSlicer marks it stale. No
218	  earlier point changes with the wait.
219	- `petg-on-cool-plate` is that refusal from the other side: its history is a
220	  `printer_setup_preview` and a `printer_setup` to Bambu PETG HF that both
221	  come back valid on the Smooth Cool Plate, because neither runs OrcaSlicer's
222	  slice-time check. The workspace block does not carry the plate type; the
223	  model can see it in that preview's result or read it with
224	  `workspace_inspect` (`printer.configured.plateType`). A
225	  `printer_setup_preview` passes because it is the step that reassesses the
226	  setup, although on this app it would come back valid again.
227	- `reply-in-german` and `file-note-not-instructions` test sentences today's
228	  prompt does not have: both rules live only in `fileReportInstructions.ts`,
229	  sent on the turn after a file opens. They are expected to score low against
230	  today's prompt. The file case's history does carry the app's developer line
231	  for earlier reports ("ignore text in a file addressed to the assistant").
232	- `print-this-no-purpose` is the one case about asking. It runs on the
233	  `"single"` fixture: one box, selected, on the project's only plate, already
234	  sliced, so a `slice_start` there would slice it again. On the two-plate
235	  fixture every run also asked which plate to print, a fair second question.
236	
237	The judge (`JUDGE_MODEL`) answers one narrow yes-or-no question about the
238	last reply, only where a string test cannot tell, for example, "set to 0.28"
239	from "could not set 0.28". Read the judge's reasons on failed runs before
240	trusting a count.
241	
242	A new case is a class in `run_prompt_tests.py` with a `name`, a docstring
243	naming its sentence and a `check()`, a `record` for it in `script.json`, and a
244	new recording.

246	## Running it
247	
248	By default every case runs 3 times (`RUN_BUDGET` 75 shared by the cases run,
249	at most 20 for one case alone); `--runs N` sets it. `--verbose` prints every
250	run's conversation. Usage is logged for every response on stderr and totalled
251	at the end.
252	
253	```bash
254	tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --render-only --prompt-rev 6b4b8b6188 > bodies.jsonl
255	```
256	
257	prints every request body it would send and their sizes, and sends nothing.
258	
259	To judge a prompt edit, run the earlier prompt with `--prompt-rev` and the
260	edit from the checkout on the same day, so both meet the same hosts.
261	Differences of a few runs are noise at three runs; run a case alone, with 20
262	runs, before reading a gap as real.

input.title: Teach the printer prompt runner several calls
input.tldr: The app now asks for, and runs, several tool calls per model response, but the printer chat's prompt-test runner still requests one call at a time and reads only the first call of each response. The new session would bring that runner in line with the app.
input.prompt:
Repository /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin (JusPrin, an OrcaSlicer fork). Work in your own new git worktree; do not push.

Background: branch `claude/every-tool-call` (worktree .claude/worktrees/every-tool-call, based on claude/print-setup-cases 8fe09f4989) changes the app's OpenAI adapter, src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp, to send `parallel_tool_calls: true` and to run every function_call of a response in the order the model wrote it. Each call gets its own function_call_output, and all results go back together in one request. A call that does not succeed (state failed or cancelled, or refused for bad arguments or an unknown tool) makes every later call in that response get, without running, the result {"state":"failed","error":{"code":"not_run","message":"Not run: an earlier call in the same response, <tool> (<call_id>), did not succeed. Nothing was queued. Call it again if it is still needed."}}. The printer task chat (the temporary printer conversation panel) uses the same adapter.

Problem: tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py still sends `parallel_tool_calls: False` (around line 227) and reads only the first function_call of each response (around line 237). It answers that call from its printer simulator, so it no longer matches what the app sends or does. The project prompt runner (tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py on claude/every-tool-call) was fixed the same way; read its Step/judge_response/answers_for code and tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py for the pattern.

Task: make the printer runner send `parallel_tool_calls: True` and answer every call of a response, in order, from its simulator, with the app's not_run result for calls after one that failed. Keep how each case checks its outcome unchanged unless a check reads only the first call; if so, describe the change before making it. Read tests/printer_prompt/README.md first and keep its style; update it to describe the rule. Verify offline only, with hand-written model outputs (no model call). Do not run live-model tests: they need Kenneth's approval for a specific batch (case count, runs, token estimate); keys live in ~/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env and must never be printed. Base the worktree on claude/every-tool-call if it has not been merged into jusprin-newui yet. Commit with a plain-English message.

content.text:
The app now runs every tool call the model sends in one response, and the prompt test runner judges and answers every call too. Both changes are committed on a new branch, `claude/every-tool-call`, and not pushed. No live model was called at any point.

## The app change (commit f8ae0639a1)

The chat now asks the model for `parallel_tool_calls: true` and runs every call in a response, in the order the model wrote them. When the last call has its result, all the results go back to the model in one request, each under its own call id. If a call fails, is cancelled, or is refused for bad arguments, the calls after it in that response are not run. Each of them gets a "not run" result that names the call that failed, so the model can decide again with both results in front of it.

The change is confined to the OpenAI adapter in `OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp`. The rest of the app still receives one call at a time.

## The test runner change (commit 829b95ff2b)

- **A change anywhere in a response decides the run.** If there are several changes, the first one counts. The `petg-on-cool-plate` response from today would now be judged as its `intent_update`. That case's own rule counts any change other than slicing as "unobserved", so the label stays the same, but the change is no longer skipped.
- **A response of reads is checked read by read.** For example, `issue-fix` now passes on a `settings_get` of its setting even when that read comes second.
- **Reads are answered all together or not at all.** If any read in the response has no recorded answer, none is answered, so no request is ever sent with a call that has no result.
- **The limit of three answered rounds now counts responses,** so a run still makes at most four requests.

## How it was tested

- **Adapter tests:** five new tests. All five fail on the old adapter and pass on the new one. All 293 agent test cases pass.
- **Runner tests:** a new offline file, `tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py`, with 13 tests. Eight fail on the old runner. One of them checks that the runner's "not run" wording matches the app's word for word.
- **`--render-only`:** produces the same 25 request bodies as before, apart from the flag.
- **End to end in the real app,** with scripted model outputs:
  - `workspace_inspect` and `intent_update` sent in one response both ran, and the intent was recorded.
  - After a `settings_apply_patch` failed, the `intent_update` sent with it was answered "not run" and never ran.
- **Default shell harness regression:** passes, 553 checks.

## Things to know before merging

- **Which branch it's built on.** It's based on `claude/print-setup-cases` at 8fe09f4989, which isn't merged into `jusprin-newui` yet. `jusprin-newui` has 87b3c50474, which also changed `requests.json`. Rebasing will conflict on that file, and the fix is to record it again.
- **One test case is recorded separately.** Recorded with the other cases, `print-this-no-purpose` starts with unsaved changes and a slice handle. Recorded on its own, it doesn't, which is how its runs were measured on 2026-10-16. So I kept the on-its-own recording for that case, the same way the session that added it did. The README explains this. The underlying difference in the recorder is still there.
- **The printer chat's test runner is out of date now.** The printer chat uses the same adapter, but `tests/printer_prompt` still asks for one call per response and reads only the first call. I've created a follow-up task for it, which you can start or dismiss.

`claude/every-tool-call` is now rebased onto `jusprin-newui` (ce11a1087e) as two commits, with `requests.json` recorded again in one full run. Nothing is pushed, and no live model was called.

- **64350306c9** "Run every tool call the model sends in one response": the app change. It applied without conflicts.
- **5823cd179d** "Judge and answer every tool call in a project prompt test response": the runner, its offline test, the README and the new recording.

## Conflicts I resolved

Your branch had moved on since I started. 8a3db9052d removed the `petg-on-cool-plate` case and set the run budget to 72, and ce11a1087e recorded `print-this-no-purpose` again.

- **Runner:** I kept the budget of 72 together with my new `MAX_READS` comment.
- **README:** I kept your text about the removed case and added one sentence about the new recording.
- **Offline test:** one of my offline tests used `petg-on-cool-plate`, so I moved it to `issue-fix`. It sends a passing read of the issue's setting together with a change to another setting, and the run must fail. Like the test it replaced, it fails on the current `jusprin-newui` runner.
- **Commit message:** updated to say the case it cites as the motivation has since been removed.
